h1: Is Red 40 safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Red 40 in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Red 40 is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Red 40, also known as Allura Red AC, is a synthetic petroleum-derived dye used to give food a bright red or orange-red color. It belongs to the azo dye family and is approved by the FDA under the designation FD&C Red No. 40. In the European Union it carries the E-number E129 and is permitted under EU food law, though products containing it must display an on-pack warning stating it may affect the activity and attention of children.

On ingredient labels, Red 40 appears under several names: Allura Red, Allura Red AC, FD&C Red No. 40, and E129. In the United States, certified color additives like Red 40 must be declared by their specific name on the label — you will not find it hidden inside a generic term like "artificial color" on domestic products. International products may list only the E-number. "May contain artificial colors" statements appear on some products manufactured on shared lines.

Foods most likely to contain Red 40: candy, fruit-flavored drinks, breakfast cereals, flavored chips and crackers, gelatin desserts, fruit-flavored yogurt, flavored snack cakes, maraschino cherries, sports drinks.

If you are avoiding Red 40 — whether for a dietary protocol, personal preference, or a household rule about artificial dyes — the challenge is finding it quickly across every product you pick up. It appears in many categories where the front-of-pack color does not make synthetic dye obvious. h1: Is Yellow 5 safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Yellow 5 in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Yellow 5 is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Yellow 5, also known as Tartrazine, is a synthetic azo dye derived from petroleum. It is used to produce yellow, green-yellow, and lime-green shades in processed food and beverages. The FDA designates it FD&C Yellow No. 5, and it carries the European E-number E102. As one of the most widely used food colorants worldwide, it appears in both food and non-food products such as medications and dietary supplements.

On labels, Yellow 5 may appear as: Tartrazine, FD&C Yellow No. 5, E102, or CI 19140. The FDA requires that Yellow 5 be declared by name on any food label — it cannot be grouped under the catch-all term "artificial color" in the United States. In the EU, products containing E102 must carry an advisory stating it may affect the activity and attention of children. Cross-reactive sensitivity with aspirin has been documented in some individuals, which is why regulatory agencies require explicit label declaration.

Foods most likely to contain Yellow 5: flavored soft drinks, candy, flavored chips, breakfast cereals, mustard, pickles, flavored gelatin, pasta mixes, fruit-flavored snacks.

Label scanning for Yellow 5 is complicated because it appears in product categories where a yellow hue looks natural — mustard, pickles, lemon-flavored items — making manual identification easy to miss. h1: Is Carrageenan safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Carrageenan in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Carrageenan is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Carrageenan is a polysaccharide extracted from red seaweed. It functions as a thickener, gelling agent, and stabilizer in processed food — it gives products a smooth, uniform texture and prevents ingredient separation. The FDA classifies carrageenan as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) for use in food. It is distinct from degraded carrageenan (poligeenan), which is not approved for food use and should not be confused with food-grade carrageenan on labels.

On ingredient labels, carrageenan appears most commonly as the single word "carrageenan." It may occasionally be qualified as "Irish moss extract" in natural-foods contexts, though that labeling is less common in mainstream products. There are no alternative E-numbers in US labeling — the FDA requires the name "carrageenan" to appear. In the EU, it carries E407 (carrageenan) or E407a (processed eucheuma seaweed). The Autoimmune Protocol (AIP) and some gut-health elimination diets exclude carrageenan from compliant food lists, making label vigilance particularly important for those following these protocols.

Foods most likely to contain carrageenan: plant-based milk alternatives, infant formula, deli meats, chocolate milk, cottage cheese, sour cream, flavored yogurt, processed soups, salad dressings.

For those following AIP, a low-inflammation diet, or any protocol that excludes carrageenan, the difficulty is that it appears in products marketed as healthy or natural — plant-based milks, organic yogurts — where it is not intuitively expected. h1: Is Yellow 6 safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Yellow 6 in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Yellow 6 is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Yellow 6, also called Sunset Yellow FCF, is a synthetic petroleum-derived azo dye that produces an orange-yellow color. The FDA designates it FD&C Yellow No. 6. In the European Union it carries the E-number E110. Like other certified synthetic color additives in the US, Yellow 6 must be listed by its full name on food labels — it cannot appear simply as "artificial color" on domestically sold products.

On labels, Yellow 6 may appear as: Sunset Yellow FCF, FD&C Yellow No. 6, E110, or CI 15985. In the EU, products containing E110 must carry the same advisory language required for all six "Southampton Six" azo dyes — a warning that it may affect the activity and attention of children. In US labeling, the FDA requires explicit name declaration. Yellow 6 is often found alongside other synthetic dyes (particularly Red 40 and Yellow 5) in products that require a multicolor effect, meaning a single product can contain several dyes at once.

Foods most likely to contain Yellow 6: flavored soft drinks, candy, flavored chips and snacks, breakfast cereals, flavored gelatin, baked goods with orange frosting, macaroni and cheese mixes, flavored popcorn.

Because Yellow 6 frequently co-occurs with Red 40 and Yellow 5, scanning one product may reveal multiple synthetic dyes simultaneously. h1: Is Sodium Nitrate safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Sodium Nitrate in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Sodium Nitrate is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Sodium nitrate is an inorganic salt used in food primarily as a curing agent and color fixative. In processed and cured meats, it helps preserve the product by inhibiting the growth of certain bacteria and stabilizing the characteristic pink-red color of cured meat. The FDA permits sodium nitrate as a direct food additive with defined use limits in specific food categories. Sodium nitrate is chemically related to sodium nitrite — the two compounds are often discussed together, though they behave differently in food and are listed separately on labels.

On labels, sodium nitrate appears as "sodium nitrate" or under the E-number E251 in EU-labeled products. Sodium nitrite (E250) is a related but distinct compound that also appears in cured meats — the two are listed separately when both are present. Products marketed as "uncured" may use natural sources of nitrates such as celery juice powder or beet juice concentrate; these are functionally equivalent curing agents but are labeled differently. Regulatory agencies require explicit labeling of both sodium nitrate and sodium nitrite when added as direct additives.

Foods most likely to contain sodium nitrate: cured deli meats, hot dogs, bacon, smoked fish, sausages, canned ham, fermented and dried meats, canned meat spreads.

For those following dietary protocols that restrict processed meats, or for label-conscious consumers watching curing agent intake, identifying sodium nitrate requires checking both the direct additive listing and the "uncured" alternative ingredient list. h1: Is Xanthan Gum safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Xanthan Gum in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Xanthan Gum is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Xanthan gum is a polysaccharide produced through bacterial fermentation of simple sugars by the microorganism Xanthomonas campestris. It functions as a thickener, stabilizer, and emulsifier — it prevents ingredient separation, gives products a consistent texture, and is used extensively in gluten-free baking as a structural substitute for gluten. The FDA classifies xanthan gum as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). It is approved under E415 in the EU.

On labels, xanthan gum appears as "xanthan gum" or E415. It does not have widely used alternative names. One nuance for specific dietary protocols: xanthan gum is produced via fermentation and the substrate (the sugar source) can vary by manufacturer — corn, wheat, or soy sugars are common feedstocks. Residual allergen carry-over from the fermentation substrate is generally considered negligible by regulatory standards, but people with severe sensitivities sometimes investigate the source. For the FODMAP diet, xanthan gum in large amounts may be a consideration, though typical food-use quantities are small.

Foods most likely to contain xanthan gum: gluten-free baked goods, salad dressings, sauces, plant-based milk alternatives, ice cream, protein shakes, meal-replacement products, smoothie mixes.

For those on strict elimination diets that flag fermented or processed additives, or who are monitoring xanthan gum intake, it appears frequently in products labeled "gluten-free" or "natural" — categories that may otherwise seem low-additive. h1: Is BHA/BHT safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: BHA/BHT in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what BHA/BHT is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
BHA (butylated hydroxyanisole) and BHT (butylated hydroxytoluene) are synthetic antioxidants used as preservatives to prevent fats and oils in food from oxidizing and going rancid. They extend the shelf life of fat-containing products significantly. The FDA classifies both BHA and BHT as GRAS when used within defined concentration limits. BHA carries EU E-number E320; BHT carries E321. The two are often used together or interchangeably depending on the application, which is why they are commonly discussed as a pair — but they are chemically distinct and listed separately on labels.

On labels, these compounds appear as "BHA," "BHT," "butylated hydroxyanisole," "butylated hydroxytoluene," E320, or E321. They may appear in the ingredient list or in a parenthetical note inside another ingredient (for example, "vegetable shortening (contains BHT)"). This nested listing is a common reason consumers miss them — the outer ingredient name is scanned, but the additive inside it is overlooked without a full text read. BHA and BHT appear on the Environmental Working Group's watch list and are flagged by several consumer dietary protocols.

Foods most likely to contain BHA/BHT: crackers, chips, cereals, chewing gum, cooking oils, shortening, instant potato products, dried soup mixes, flavored nuts, packaged baked goods.

h1: Is TBHQ safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: TBHQ in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what TBHQ is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
TBHQ stands for tertiary butylhydroquinone, a synthetic antioxidant used as a fat preservative. It prevents oxidation in oils, fats, and fat-rich food products, extending shelf life and preventing rancidity. The FDA approves TBHQ as a food additive with defined maximum use levels — it must not exceed 0.02% of the fat or oil content in a product. In the European Union, TBHQ is not permitted as a food additive, which makes it a compound that appears in US-sold products but would be absent from equivalents manufactured for the EU market.

On labels, TBHQ appears as "TBHQ" or "tertiary butylhydroquinone." Like BHA and BHT, it can appear either as a standalone ingredient entry or nested inside a fat or oil sub-ingredient disclosure in parentheses. The EU prohibition creates a notable divergence: some international or imported products that do not use TBHQ may be reformulated versions of US products that do. Domestic products destined for export to the EU require reformulation, which means a "same brand" product purchased in the US versus abroad may have a different preservative profile.

Foods most likely to contain TBHQ: fast-food fried items (oils), microwave popcorn, crackers, chips, instant noodles, frozen fish sticks, peanut butter products, cooking sprays.

TBHQ's presence in fried and oil-heavy foods makes it particularly easy to miss — the front of pack often emphasizes protein content or whole-grain claims rather than preservative disclosure. h1: Is Carmine safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Carmine in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Carmine is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Carmine is a red colorant derived from the dried bodies of the cochineal insect, a scale insect that lives on cactus plants. The color compound itself is carminic acid. In food, carmine produces stable pink, red, and purple shades and is used as an alternative to synthetic red dyes. The FDA classifies carmine as a color additive that must be declared by name on food labels — a rule implemented specifically because some individuals may experience allergic reactions to it and because of its animal-derived origin, which makes it relevant to vegan and certain religious dietary practices.

On labels, carmine may appear as "carmine," "cochineal extract," "carminic acid," "natural red 4," or E120 (the EU E-number). Prior to a 2011 FDA rule change, carmine was sometimes grouped under "artificial colors" or "color added" without explicit identification — the current requirement for name disclosure was introduced to address labeling transparency concerns. For people following vegan diets, carmine is a non-plant-derived ingredient that is not always obvious from its name alone, as it does not reference its insect source.

Foods most likely to contain carmine: strawberry and raspberry-flavored yogurt, fruit punch and berry drinks, flavored candy, maraschino cherries, processed meat (sausage casings), some alcoholic beverages, frozen novelties, flavored milk.

Carmine's multiple label names — particularly "cochineal extract" and "natural red 4" — make it a common miss for label readers who know to avoid "carmine" but do not recognize the synonyms. h1: Is Titanium Dioxide safe? What you need to know before eating it.
metaTitle: Titanium Dioxide in food: what it is & how to avoid it — Nouri
metaDescription: Find out what Titanium Dioxide is, why it's in food, which products contain it, and how Nouri scans for it automatically. Free iOS app.
bodyContent:
Titanium dioxide is an inorganic white pigment used in food to produce a bright white color and to improve the visual opacity of products. In food applications it is used in extremely small quantities as a colorant and opacifying agent. The FDA classifies titanium dioxide as an approved color additive for food use when added at a level not exceeding 1% by weight. In the European Union, titanium dioxide (E171) was banned as a food additive in August 2022 following a re-evaluation by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), which concluded that it could no longer be considered safe in food due to concerns related to its nanoparticle form — creating a regulatory divergence between the US and EU.

On labels, titanium dioxide appears as "titanium dioxide" or E171. The EU ban means that products reformulated for the European market will not contain it, while the same product sold in the US may still list it. This creates a situation where consumers traveling internationally or purchasing imported goods may encounter different formulations of the same brand. The EU prohibition applies specifically to food; titanium dioxide remains permitted in cosmetics and non-food products in the EU under different regulations.

Foods most likely to contain titanium dioxide: white candy coating and confectionery glazes, chewing gum, powdered sugar products, white frosting, salad dressings, non-dairy coffee creamers, certain processed cheeses, white-coated dietary supplements.

Titanium dioxide is easy to overlook because it appears in categories — confections, dressings, creamers — where a plain-white color seems unremarkable. Nouri flags titanium dioxide in the ingredient detail panel on every scan. Nouri scans for Titanium Dioxide automatically — free on iOS.
